consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on the garden as Eden/paradise: the place of God's presence, life, and unbroken communion with humanity, lost through sin and eschatologically restored (Genesis 2-3 through Revelation 22). Common secondary layers include the temple-sanctuary reading, the bride/Church/soul allegory from the Song of Songs, the watered-garden image of fruitfulness, and Johannine/Gethsemane new-creation typology.
book_summary: The book defines a garden as 'a planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations,' building on its separate symbol equation of trees with nations (cross-referencing its Trees chapter) and citing Ezekiel 31:9, where the trees of Eden in the garden of God envy the Assyrian cedar. It explicitly flags the paradise/Eden-lost-and-restored reading as the 'commonly taught' view it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: Garden = paradise/Eden as the place of God's presence and communion with humanity, lost at the Fall and restored in the new creation.
book_core_identification: Garden = a grouping of nations (a planted stand of trees, where each tree symbolizes a nation).
boundary_disagreement: Not a boundary dispute: the book does not narrow or extend the paradise reading; it substitutes a corporate-geopolitical referent (a collection of nations) for the consensus's theological-relational referent (place of divine presence/communion). Passages the consensus treats as paradise imagery (Eden, Revelation 22, Song of Songs) would be reclassified under the book's scheme as depictions of assembled nations, and none of the consensus's alternatives (temple, bride/soul, fruitful life, Gethsemane typology) anticipates this.
material_contradiction: The book's own common-view note acknowledges and sets aside the paradise/fellowship-with-God identification. 'Place of God's presence and communion with humanity' and 'a grouping of nations' cannot both be the core symbolic identification of 'garden' in the same sense and context; accepting the book's definition requires replacing the consensus identification rather than refining it.
rationale: Reduced to minimum cores, consensus says garden symbolizes paradise/divine presence; the book says garden symbolizes an assembly of nations. These are different referents, not different precisions of the same referent. The book leans on Ezekiel 31, where trees genuinely function as figures for nations/rulers (Assyria as a great cedar, other 'trees of Eden' as nations), and generalizes that local metaphor into the master definition of 'garden.' No consensus response or alternative lists a 'nations' reading, but because the book directly displaces the acknowledged common teaching rather than merely adding an unlisted layer, DIVERGENT rather than NOVEL is correct.
strongest_objection: Ezekiel 31 demonstrably uses tree imagery for nations and places those trees 'in the garden of God,' so one could argue the book is only isolating a legitimate context-specific usage (as Response B notes, garden meaning is context-dependent), making this an unlisted complementary layer (NOVEL or even REFINED) rather than a replacement. But the entry offers the nations reading as the definition of the symbol and explicitly contrasts it with the commonly taught paradise view, which is displacement, not layering. The single cited verse supports trees-as-nations more directly than garden-as-grouping-of-nations, and cannot by itself carry the generalization across Genesis, Song of Songs, and Revelation — hence only partial citation support.
